utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could retrieve please Exhibit P328, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, if we could briefly finish the orientation about locations of settlements in Dobrinja. Without making these circles, although they look very, very fancy, can you please just mark with numbers the other settlements in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This settlement is Dobrinja 2-B, between the river and the Dobrinja D-1; this one is D-1, D 1-2; then Dobrinja 2-1 and Dobrinja 2-A. Next to this settlement is a village or some old houses which used to be in Dobrinja before the building blocks began being built; then at the foot of Mojmilo hill, we have Dobrinja 3-B and next to it 3-A. At the entrance to the Dobrinja settlement, next to the road, is Dobrinja 5, or D-5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President if this -- the previous exhibit which was P328, the one which was marked for identification last -- yesterday, could be tendered as an exhibit and also this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday's exhibit, which was marked for identification, will now be Exhibit P328, and today' marking will be Exhibit P329.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just for the record, the markings the witness has added today are in blue, while yesterday the markings were in red. If we could have a new exhibit, in fact, it's the original one, ter number 03013, please. And this is the last page of that 19-page range; again, the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Witness, while that is being retrieved, this is the same exhibit that you see on the ELMO, and you're very familiar with this one. Can you please explain to the Judge what is these red lines mean. And, first, I want to talk about the red line, and you might want to turn to the ELMO, the red line that is kind of vertical from Mojmilo, the settlement down towards the airport, and cutting off parts of what you call the airport settlement, yesterday. That's this twisted line on the left side of the plan. I would like to you indicate to Your Honours what that is, but we need to wait until we have the image appearing on your screen. And unlike yesterday, today we will have a red line as it appears in the original, so there's no need to -- to mark it again. And just a look at the ELMO, you see the red line there on your ELMO on your right side?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Your Honours what line that is. What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This line in the airport settlement is the separation line. This is where we had contact with the Serb forces. They were across the road, and these were our positions in the airport settlement. On the other side of the line, there were the Serb forces just across the street. This settlement was attacked between the 16th and the 21st of June. People were forced out, and the civilians were forced to go to the rest of Dobrinja; whereas, part of them was taken across the airport to Kula, the other portion of the inhabitants remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you can now turn to the screen, because we do have the line now on your screen. Do you see the line that goes vertically down from Mojmilo settlement down towards the airport?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From here down to the airport, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's the line you just were making comments about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one. The other one inside the airport settlement. What I see on the ELMO is another line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Please concentrate on the line that we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if the picture could be enlarged, please. The picture on the screen. I'm sorry. So we see the wider area, so I guess it's the way it was in the original state. So I guess making smaller so the whole area can be seen. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, please explain, again, the line the one that you see on the left side from Mojmilo down towards the airport settlement.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From here, we have the separation line between our forces and the Serb forces through the settlement of Dobrinja 5, the river, and the village there towards the airport settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And can you -- because it's not easy for us to follow you, you have to make a little marking. Can you make a little cross at the line you're looking now.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm putting the cross in the central part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's a blue cross and we have seen it now. So that depicts the separation line between your forces and the Serbian forces. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's now turn to the other red line on the right side of the screen, and if you can make another marking depicting the line on the right side.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a blue cross. It is the separation line between Dobrinja and Oslobodenje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on which side were your forces?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that where the word "Mojmilo" is written?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you now move totally to the right side of the screen. Do you see another red line coming from Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you make another marking, and please attach the letter C to this other marking.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small arrow and the letter C.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. What does this red line depict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This red line is the separation line between our and Serbian forces. Our forces are inside the line towards the arrow; whereas, the Serb forces were on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you go down that red line, after about, in centimetres, 5, 6 centimetres, there is a horizontal line just below the word "Dobrinja," ending with a dot and two dashes. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see "Dobrinja" marking the river on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And if you follow that red line, can you see the word "Dobrinja" and a red dot below the word "Dobrinja"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is exactly on the spot where I put the dot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And can you explain to Your Honours what this additional red line that goes off the vertical red line signifies?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, we did not have this additional line or position. Since this was an abandoned school and it was no man's land, during the war, we extended our positions so as to try and prevent the Serbian forces to enter the elementary school mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you encircle the elementary school, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hadzic. Now, if we go back to the centre of the -- the chart, there is a red line which crosses the airport. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the line that I will put a blue dot next to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell Your Honours what this red line depicts, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red line represents the tunnel which we had dug under the runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was the tunnel operational?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, perhaps I could add two or three sentences by way of introduction. Since we were beseiged and given the situation for almost a year, people were trying to run across the runway, trying to either escape from the city or to return with some food for their families. It was hell. There was a grave need to make a hole of sorts, so as to try and stop the killing that took place on the runway. According to some unofficial data, in less than a year, 120 people were killed on that runway. Usually, the Serbian forces, which were below the airport, opened fire at the people trying to cross. And sometimes the IFOR or SFOR soldiers even turned their lights on the people running across, and they would make them really an easy target. And it wasn't important who was trying to cross, whether it was a child, a woman, or a young man. Since one of our members worked at the airport - he was an engineer and a Hungarian by origin - he brought us the plans, the sketches. There is -- there are drainage pipes next to the runway, which are supposed to take away the rain and takes the water further away to the riverbed nearby. From one end of the airport to another one, to the other end of the airport, there -- the diameter of those pipes was between 300 and 1.200 millimetre. By using those pipes, one could move from one end of the airport to another. Next to Aco's cafe on the other side, there was a manhole through which you could reach one end of the drainage pipes, and one could go all the way to the other end; however, that end was controlled by the Serb forces and that provided us with the original idea to make a tunnel. We began digging in early 1993. At first there were problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was it operational, when was it able to be used?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of July, 1993, the two sides met because the tunnel was being dug from two sides simultaneously. The next day one could use the tunnel, although with some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation, Mr. Hadzic. If we can return for the last time to this chart, I see there are numbers in the middle of this chart. Do you see those numbers?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With some difficulty, but, yes, I do see those: 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you can always refer to the original which is still on your ELMO. But before I ask you that question, does this chart with the red lines you discussed a moment ago, does display the situation, the confrontation lines were in summer 1994 and later?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the line at Mojmilo, which until 1994 was next to the road, the rest of the lines were as shown here. Only at the end of 1994 and beginning of 1995, we moved the Mojmilo line to the top of the hill so as to join the 101st Brigade and to prevent any possible incursion towards Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for the clarification. We come to Mojmilo in a moment. Now, can you please look at number 1 and circle number 1 on the screen, and please tell us what number 1 depicts?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 is the place which the brigade command was at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was it located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located in Dobrinja 2 on -- or at a corner of a building where the Borovo shop used to be, where shoes were sold.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it in one of the apartments? Was it in the basement? Was it on the street level? How many rooms were there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor. Part of the offices were in the basement, although the conditions were poor. There was water, and it was impossible to store anything there, so the ground floor of that shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said it was initially in number 1. Did it move over time, the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 1st of August, they tried to fire from Gacica hill, trying to hit the building where we were; however, they missed and hit the adjacent building as well as some shops in between. After that, after that attempt, we moved the brigade command to another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was it moved to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the building marked with the number 2, across from the other building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And where was the headquarters in August and later of 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 and 1995, after we moved to another location, we were at number 2. In 1995, we were there; but by end 1995 when the two brigades merged, we moved to the barracks of Ramiz Salcin or Viktor Bubanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We dealt with number 2. What about number 3?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 3 was a tactical move, trying to fool the Serb forces. We moved there for a short while; and once we realised they were no longer attacking the former headquarters, we returned to number 2 because in certain aspects the location at number 2 was safer than the one at number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what number 4 was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4 is in the C5 settlement. It was a command post of the 2nd Battalion of the Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You just marked again with a blue circle the location of -- of number 4 and just above the entry to the tunnel. What was number 5?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5 is the command of the 1st Battalion. I put a blue cross next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And the last number is number 6.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 6 is in Dobrinja 5. Is the command post of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And these positions, were they also valid in late 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, were there companies subordinated to these battalions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were the companies located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the separation line. Usually, a battalion would have four companies, out of which three were always on duty and one was supposed to be the reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did they have a headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were these headquarters located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us a moment ago that your brigade headquarters was shelled. Now, in your observation, was it shelled more or less than the other areas in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither more nor less. All areas were targeted the same way. No distinction was made between a brigade command or an elementary school or a flea market for that matter, later in 1994. Shells landed everywhere with no distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could tender this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, before you leave this picture, could you please ask the witness if he could explain to us what the confrontation line looked like in this urban area. Were there barbed wire or any other physical, visible markings, and how was it possible for the local population to know exactly where the confrontation line? For the witness's information, I'm putting this question through the Prosecutor to you, Mr. Witness, because we have had many witnesses here during this trial who have told us that they were not exactly sure of where the confrontation line was. So this triggered my interest in knowing a little more about how it would be possible for a civilian to ascertain where exactly the confrontation line was. Could you help us clarify this question? I put the question through the Prosecutor because he's examining at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, witness, I think this is a very important question. Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I would be happy to. Dobrinja is an urban settlement, a modern settlement. The population of our part, that was under our control, knew exactly where our lines were as opposed to the Serbian lines. The soldiers also prevented civilians from going further in case they came to the enemy lines too close. Some people wanted to move about, trying to find firewood, but we wouldn't let them move too far so have as few casualties as possible. The 27.000 inhabitants of Dobrinja new exactly where our lines were as opposed to the Serbian lines, and they were also familiar with the exact spots where they shouldn't go or move about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In one case, you told us that the Serbian forces were just across the street. Would that mean, then, that the Muslim people would not be able to go across the street to the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if they tried to cross over, they would be killed. The airport settlement was a very characteristic one. The separation line between our forces and the Serbian forces was a road five wide. In one part of the settlement, which was under our control, there were Bosnian forces in buildings, and across the road in other buildings were the Serbian forces. Your Honour, it sometimes happened that inhabitants or our soldiers or the Serbian soldiers wanted to get a cigarette because having cigarettes was a -- like an enormous fortune at the time which helped alleviate the pain that they were suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you also answer the question by Judge Harhoff whether these confrontation lines were fortified. Did they have barbed wire? Were there other distinctive features?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any barbed wires.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could please go to map 028 -- 02872, please, and I would like to talk about Mojmilo hill now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that there was some changes to the confrontation lines at Mojmilo hill. Can you tell us what kind of feature of Mojmilo hill? How did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already said at the beginning that either on the 13th or the 15th of May, 1992, the Serbian forces took up positions on Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm mainly interested in what's happening after 1994, when you made some moves to enlarge your area of responsibility on Mojmilo hill. Can you with briefly explain us where you had soldiers stationed on Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1994, there always danger of the Serbian forces entering Mojmilo from the right flank and thereby enter our area of responsibility; that is, either 101st or the 155th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the map could be enlarged around Dobrinja. North of Dobrinja we have the word "Novi Grad," and that part should be enlarged, just south. Yes. Thank you. And if you again to the left side of the map and enlarge that part again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you see now Mojmilo hill there displayed, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you mark where the positions of your brigade were in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps it could even be made bigger, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one second, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can it be made still a little bit bigger? I think we'll leave it. It will take too much time.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In earlier 1994, we had trenches up to this point, up to this red point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Please add a letter A to the red point. A larger A, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since in 1995 the blue route was opened and we started receiving logs from Mount Igman, we decided in order to fortify the inside part of our lines to extend the line and to link it up on the top of Mojmilo with the final point of the trenches of the 101st Brigade. If you allow me, I can draw this line for you. This is where we linked up with the 101st, which definitely closed up any point of entry for the Serbian forces penetrating our area in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have soldiers up there, and where was the -- where were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We deployed part of the 1st Battalion in the trenches in order to cover this line. There was sentry points, there were machine-gun nests, and everything else which is necessary to maintain a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there an UNPROFOR position on Mojmilo hill as well?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the highest peak of Mojmilo hill, I believe. There was a medieval fortress there and observation positions of UN forces were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you depict on the map where the highest point of Mojmilo hill was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to do that on this map. I can just do it roughly and put a dot. It perhaps does not correspond exactly because this is not a topographic map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We see the idea. Can you please add letter B next to it; not on the dot, but next to the dot. Letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can briefly talk about weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'd like to tender this map as an exhibit, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P331.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You answered, yesterday, a question by Judge Harhoff about weaponry. You talked mainly about infantry weaponry. Did you have, in terms of mortars, did you have in your brigade in Dobrinja 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first 81 mortar was donated to us by the 4th Motorised Brigade in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. Did you have 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dobrinja, no, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let's talk about this 81-millimetre mortar you just started to talk about. You said you received one in October 1993. Did you ever use this mortar in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a 181-millimetre calibre, but we never had shells for it; however, we did use it to train our men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have 60-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In earlier 1994, when an offensive on Mount Igman started, we had 120-millimetre mortars, as well as 60-millimetre mortars, which we deployed in the area of responsibility of the Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thought the witness said --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, let me clarify. Did you use 120-millimetre mortars in Dobrinja, or did you use it, if you had them, outside of Dobrinja at Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can are remember, not in Dobrinja. We didn't use 120-millimetres mortars, but we did use them on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many 60-millimetre mortars did you have in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, each company had two to four 60-millimetre mortars. They were positioned opposite the company in order to cover the separation line in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what's the range of a 60-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, between 1.000 and 1.500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did you have guns? I mean heavy guns as opposed to rifles?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for one recoilless gun, which didn't have any sights, we didn't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was the recoilless gun located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the 1st Battalion, close to the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let me go back to the -- these trenches. The purpose, the way I understand of these trenches, is obviously to defend yourself against the enemy, and these trenches were at the front lines. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we have seen that chart with the red lines. Now, was there a second line of defence which was more inside Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only the front line of defence in Dobrinja and nothing else; the front line and that's it. And all our expertise and knowledge was used on this front line, because practically it was impossible to establish any other line in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there trenches used, so-called communication trenches, used inside Dobrinja for the protection of civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian protection, with the units and men they had at their disposal, constructed or dug out communication trenches between certain settlements to allow people to move around and do -- run their errands. And these communication trenches were actually built in order to provide protection for the civilian population from fire while they were moving around and doing their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And protection against -- against whom?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did your soldiers use these trenches which were built for the protection of civilians to fire?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us about the civilian defence. Very briefly on the civilian defence, were they part of your chain of command? Were they subordinated to a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not in our chain of command. They had their own command and their own commander. All civilian protection units were subordinated to this commander and the orders that he issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Prosecutor that there was no need for your soldiers to use the trenches that had been built for the protection of civilians to fire. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Dobrinja battlefield, Your Honour, was a typical urban warfare, so to speak. The communication trenches were inside the settlement, and the separation line led from the trenches as far as 800 to 1.000 metres. Sometimes one couldn't even see the line from these trenches; therefore, it was impossible to fire from these trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you never had to fire either defensively, and you never fired aggressively.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there are two types of trenches. The first trenches, as I understand the evidence of the witness, were at the front lines used by the soldiers, and the other trenches, inside, were what he called communication trenches which you were used by the civilians to cross from one point to the other one, if that can be clarified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, would you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a while ago that the communication trenches were inside the settlement linking various parts of the settlement for the civilian purposes, for their moving around. We didn't have any barracks in Dobrinja or places where battalions or companies were billeted. After finishing their duty, each soldier would go home. However, it was impossible to launch any defensive or offensive actions, because we would jeopardise our soldiers much more than we would jeopardise the Serbian soldiers because of the position of the trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They were, as it were, internalised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that these communication trenches is internalised. Trenches were constructed by the civilian defence. Did the civilian defence do other things in order to protect the civilians from sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was possible; for example, from the central part of Dobrinja, which was covered with concrete slabs 40 by 40, we removed all those slabs in order to protect the windows at ground floors of the buildings, in order to protect them from shrapnel exploding in front of these buildings. The civilian protection also did unloading of humanitarian aid, distributed humanitarian aid. They also dug graves and organised and arranged funerals with the families. Dobrinja didn't have any burial site, so we had to make sort of improvised graveyards for the people who were killed in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. You explained the protection that was initiated by the civilian defence and others for the civilians. Now, which areas, which streets perhaps of Dobrinja were most exposed, if there any such, to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the central streets, the intersections; the main street connecting two parts of Dobrinja where there was a so-called Mitsubisi avenue, which was the biggest one, or the airport settlement, or rather, the road where a trolley-bus service was running; and all intersections where it was possible to fire upon people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And going to the other side, were there specific hot spots where sniper fire would originate from?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, and the area around Dobrinja where sniper nests would be located in your experience.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would begin from the Oslobodenje, which is the final point of defence line. The first or -- place, or rather, the house, the so-called Sandzak big red house, was a sniper nest covering the Nedzarici intersection below the dormitory and also the entrance to the Oslobodenje building. The second nest was in the centre for the blind people overlooking Alipasin and the intersection there. In Nedzarici, the most infamous place was the faculty of theology, which was on a higher ground and overlooking the entry point to Dobrinja and Mojmilo as well as the intersection at the entry point to Mojmilo. The higher ground were in Nedzarici where sniper nests could have been placed; and in Dobrinja, actually in the village on the other side held by the Serbs, there was a sniper nest in a house covering the Mitsubishi avenue, and there was another private house overlooking the road leading to Dobrinja 1. From the lower part, the most dangerous place was the bell tower of the Orthodox church and also a place in Dobrinja 4 under the control of the VRS arm. And another hot spot that caused many problems for us was the so-called Vitkovica house below Mojmilo, which covered the middle section of the Mitsubishi avenue and the area around the hospital in Dobrinja. So more or less this would be the spots that I can now remember where snipers were active from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who controlled these hot spots, as you just outlined?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these spots that I mentioned were on the side controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were these hot spots still active in the second part of 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's interesting how they operated, these people firing on people. From one point, they would be shooting for a day or two, then they would be quiet for some 15 or 20 days; and then reactivate this spot for another two or three days and that happened on a daily basis year after year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who were the targets of this sniping? Was it soldiers, civilians, other people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not -- they were indiscriminate in choosing their victims. The first victim in Dobrinja was a Serbian woman, 67 years of age. Children or elderly people, women, soldiers, even UN soldiers were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to show you one document, and that's the only one I'm using in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. President, Your Honours, this is 02306.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While that is being done, who were you subordinated to? Who was your boss?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war or -- at the beginning of the war, it was the commander of the 1st Corps of the BH army, the late General Abdullah Hajrulahovic. He was succeeded by General Karavelic; and then following the reorganisation of the army, divisions were formed, we became subordinated to General Prevljak, and at the end of the war to General Ojnadzic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this document, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If perhaps the second page could be shown which has the signature.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there is a document, or rather, documents collected by the 12th Division from its subordinate units in order to make a composite report about daily events in the area of responsibility of the 12th Division. Actually, it was General Karavelic who put all these reports together and filed them in the archives. So these were daily reports provided by units on everything that was happening on a daily basis in their representative zones of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think this document is authored by Mr. Karavelic, the person that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page again, to the first paragraph. It starts: "Aggressor." And let's just have a look at the first two sentences. "In the past 24 hours in the area of responsibility of the 12th Division, the enemy intensively fired sniper rifles and small arms on the lines of defence and civilian targets"; and then it goes on and mentions also several brigades, including the brigade 155th Mountain Brigade. That's your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It also mentions that a member of the French Battalion was killed. Now, is that an example of sniping against civilian targets that you experienced in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is the best illustration of your question. In item 2, our forces, it says, "In the area of responsibility of 155th Mountain Brigrade, one woman was killed and one was seriously injured."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the document could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit P332.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of rifles the Serbian forces used for their sniping activities?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we used to receive from some people from the UN forces, who were at the airport within their area of responsibility, when they would ask or plead with the Serbian forces not to open fire from snipers because a truce was signed, they told us that they would get information that the Serb forces usually used modern sniping rifles called Pasp, P-a-s-p, produced by the Yugoslav national army and the so-called Argentinian rifle which used the 12 point 7-millimetre bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a sniper rifle used by the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an abandoned apartment in Dobrinja next to the airport, in a building which had previously been shelled, we saw something. The blinds fell due to the shelling, and a rifle fell out of the window. It had no bullets, and it had some missing parts; however, we had some people in our logistics who worked in weapons production, and they saw the rifle fall down. They told us that this was the Pasp this rifle, this beautiful, horrible, high-tech rifle, and its parts were very modern. As for the Argentinian rifle, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is the optimal range of the PASP rifle, the optimal range of firing at targets of the PASP rifle, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People say that it achieves the best results between 800 and 1.000 metres, but it can reach as far as 1500.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If document, in fact, it is a photo, ter 02981 could be retrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While that is being done, can I ask you, did you have interaction with UNPROFOR as a commander of the Dobrinja Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And given the fact that in your area of responsibility civilians were dying, as you told us, did you protest to UNPROFOR about these instances?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the French Battalion was at the airport. Our cooperation was a fair one. We met on a weekly basis and arranged various activities; particularly, humanitarian aid delivery which went across their area towards Dobrinja. They also held regular meetings with some people on the Serbian side. We -- since we were unable to communicate in writing, but rather it was the corps command who communicated in writing with the SFOR, we asked them to ask the other side not to open sniper fire against people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "people," what do you mean? Soldiers, civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many times would you make such representations that they shouldn't open fire against civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all the time or at least very frequently. It was a major problem for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please turn your attention to the screen please, to the photo. Do you know what it depicts, what it shows?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. It is the Simone Bolivar elementary school, and my children used to attend that school before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take it that's the building in the middle, which has a sort of a dark brown roof?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident in May 1994 -- 1995 when the school was shelled, and there were casualties, civilian casualties? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I wasn't present at Dobrinja at that time, but I was told that in the flower or greenery garden, as we called it, a shell landed and that there were nine wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I know it's difficult to cast back your mind, but do you recall whether there was any combat activity around the school or in the vicinity on the day that that happened?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that exactly. I think it was in May 1995 when the focus was on the Igman/Treskavica plateau. I don't think there was any combat in Dobrinja itself at that time. Of course, I may stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, the incident occurred on the 18th of June, 1995. Does that refresh your recollection of that incident better?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is the 18th of June, then there was little likelihood that there was anything happening in Dobrinja. It was on the 18th of June, 1995. The preparations to block the city of Sarajevo were under way; therefore, the focus was up there at Igman and Bjelasnicka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you see the brigade headquarters of your brigade on this picture.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It Cannot be seen here, but one can see the building where the command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you encircle the building where the command was, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The witness has marked the building at the bottom of the picture with a large red circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be admitted as an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P333.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You appear to have under estimated the time for this witness, because two and a half hours were allotted, both for examination-in-chief and cross-examination, and you have already used up one hour and 12 minutes but plus 45. So that is one hour, 57 minutes, but of course his evidence is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, I have a question for the witness, please. Witness, please, you were a commander of a brigade, and I'm sure, as such, you know that something that many experts told us. Many experts told us that sniping is a normal activity of Armed Forces; sniping against military targets, of course, and not sniping against civilians. But sniping against military targets is authorised. So, yourself, in your own brigade, did you also have snipers? Did you also have marksmen sniping the Serbs, the Serb forces. So I'm asking this question because I like to know whether there was any cross-fire. Because yesterday when you answered one of my questions, you said that your brigade had been set up to protect civilians against the Serb forces. So I tend to imagine for that reason that you probably also had sniper -- snipers who were shooting at the other side, and that may be there could have been collateral damage that could explain problems that could have happened; notably, regarding what happened to the school that we see here in this photograph. Because from the photograph, it looks like the school is very close to the command post of your own brigade. I'm just trying to think this out, to understand what happened, and I would like your help in this regard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd be happy to. At the brigade and in the zone of responsibility, we had no classical marksmen. But we had people at positions who had rifles, and they could be turned into marksmen should there be such a need. As for your other question whether they indeed fired, well, Dobrinja has good acoustics because of the buildings, but cannot determine where the firing came from. But people tried to assess where the firing came from, and they would then open fire at those buildings from the trenches we had. However, I want to stress, and I agree with you that sniping is something deemed necessary in combat activities, but it only applies to the opposing forces. If one kills a girl in an apartment or a girl playing in front of a building or to kill an old woman doing laundry at the river or an old man who came out to smoke a cigarette or catch some fresh air, then that is certainly not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not quite satisfied with the when given by the witness, and maybe if we reformulate the question we can have a better answer. The allegation, of course, is that it has been brought to the Chamber's attention that sniping also took place from areas held by the Bosnian army. And so the question to be put to you, Mr. Witness, if you are aware of any such sniping fire being launched from the area under your responsibility, and also the question is whether snipers under your command had weapons of precision; that is to say, sniper weapons. I did ask you yesterday if you had any weaponry, and I was told that you had only old hunting rifles and small weapons, and now we hear that actually the battalions under your command were in possession of 60-millimetre mortars. Now, I would have expected you to give me that answer when I put the question to you yesterday. So I kindly ask you now to give a thorough and full answer to the questions posed by the Bench. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd be happy to. Yesterday, when you asked me about the weaponry, I understood you were asking me about the very beginning of the war, and I provided the accurate answer. We received 60-millimetre mortars in late 1993 or early 1994. At the brigade, we did not have snipers. We had no precision rifles that could be used for sniping; however, we had some marksmen at the front line who had hunting rifles that could be turned into sniping rifles should there be such a need. They probably opened fire on the other side, acting as snipers, but we never issued such orders, and we strictly forbade opening fire on any targets other than soldiers. I hope this suffices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying that the sniping rifles you had were not precision rifles, as you had seen from the other side? Because you did see sniping rifle from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And one could tell that these people were professionals. I have no document or information to corroborate that. But the rumour had it that in 1994/1995, in the Sarajevo area of responsibility, the so-called weekend warriors came. They were professionals from the neighbouring countries of Romania, Macedonia, Belarus, and they would come and fight over the weekends for 2.000 German marks each, and then they would take that home with the money and go home. Sometimes our soldiers joked that the best shooters we had at the front line were the people who poached before the war. Poaching means when you hunt illegally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did I also understand you to say that any sniping rifles held by your side would have been a hunting rifle that was converted to a sniping rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Your Honour. Your Honour, the closest thing that comes to that definition is the hunting rifles that the hunters possessed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to turn on the other microphone as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would the usher see that the other microphone for the witness is turned on. So you never had a rifle that was in and of itself a sniping rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not of such quality as the Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you did have proper sniping rifles, as opposed to a normal hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I understand you have said that you had hunting rifles which could be turned into a sniping rifle.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way. Those hunting rifles did not have optical sights such as a sniping rifle would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And apart from those hunting rifles that were used as sniping rifles, did you have any other sniping rifles with the appropriate telescopic features?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer this way, and I'll do my best. Given the situation we were in, and given the balance of strength at Dobrinja, any weapon we had, even automatic rifles, could be used for sniping, because sometimes the distance was as little as eight metres. If you able to see the soldier on the other side, you could use a handgun to kill him. But we had no modern rifles that should or are supposed to be used originally for sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you mentioned a moment ago what you called weekend fighters and that they were paid a couple of thousand German marks. Who paid, and I understand these are rumours, but did the rumours tell you who paid the money to these weekend fighters.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were on the other side, it would be illogical for to us pay them to kill us. They were paid by the military structures of the army of Republika Srpska or the civilian structures of Republika Srpska, the authorities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who would allow these snipers to come to the front lines? Did the rumours also tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. But logically speaking, approaching a front line can only be approved by the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, shall we permit rumours in such important matters, and can anyone stand by rumours? This is a question have I for the Bench. These are serious matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will clarify how that information was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you started saying that you have heard information, but there was no documents to substantiate that. That's how you prefaced your kind of volunteering this information. Can you tell what was the basis for the information that these people from Romania or Macedonia might have come to snipe at people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our intelligence gained such information through some people, who at the end of 1993 and 1994 and in 1995 managed to flee, previously having been caught and detained close to our area of responsibility. They were later used as a workforce in the area of responsibility of the Dobrinja Brigade. For example, five or six people fled from Bosanska Krupa and the area of Kula, and they conveyed that information to our intelligence officers. They told them about the arrivals of these weekend warriors. We gained that information through such people. I cannot tell you anything concerning the veracity of it, but this is what our they told our intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, I don't have too much-- just to continue onto a couple of issues. Now, were the Serbs, who laid, you know, siege on Dobrinja or who encircled Dobrinja, were they able to observe Dobrinja from their positions around Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. They were at various elevations, and they controlled 80 percent of all movement in Dobrinja. On the left side, at Mojmilo hill, from that elevation one sees one third of Dobrinja. At Trebevic, there is a telecommunication tower; and with a good sights, you can see all of Dobrinja, and then Grbavicka Brdo to the right, which commands at least two thirds of Dobrinja, provided you have good equipment, you can monitor all movement and all activity in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. You have spoken about the sniping and shelling of civilians in Dobrinja and that there were casualties among the civilians. Now, how did, based on your observations, how did the civilians cope, specifically did you observe whether or not the shooting and shelling of civilians impacted on them psychologically.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, it was a disaster, psychologically speaking. It affected not only the people who were killed and their families but the entire neighbourhood around the area where someone had been killed. In 1994 and 1995, it became a normal thing, although to say that it was normal is horrific. Only the families who had their family members killed were affected. But as for the others, they just saw one person less. That was the mental state of the population. Death was the most common thing in 1994 and 1995; although, the psychological burden was somewhat less than in the initial two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if you have just another few minutes, then we'll continue; if not, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. I have just one more question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I hear the French channel, but perhaps that could be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You know that the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from August 1994 was General Galic; is that correct? Sorry, General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also know that the predecessor was General Galic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you meet any of these commanders during the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see General Milosevic here today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on the ground, you were the commander in -- of the Dobrinja Brigade in Dobrinja. Did you see change when General Milosevic took over from General Galic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I was a soldier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think the problem question should be: Was there a change when General Milosevic took over; and if so, please describe its characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To say "did you see change" is very misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a change, as you could observe from your position on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not a professional soldier. I am an engineer, a technical person, and that's how I see things in life. I noticed the way the war was waged, and I had the feeling that General Milosevic could exercise more freedom than General Galic had previously. He could go one step further in his command. By the end of the war, my assessment, of course, could have changed, but I was of the view that they used a more systematic approach. They targeted the infrastructure and anything of importance for ordinary life. There were two boiler rooms which had previously been damaged, but in 1995 they put them out of operation completely. The central part of Dobrinja has local heating facility on a roof, and they targeted those heating facilitates and the boiler rooms to put them out of work, out of operation. They also targeted intersections, roads, trying to achieve maximum effect. There was another thing -- was the use of vollies, whereby you would have four, six, or eight shells fall to the same place covering the total distance of 100 metres, simply leveling that place. I think those were the differences. And at the end, I could see that he could exercise more freedom in his command than General Galic had. General Galic had the General Staff above him; but close to the end of the war, I was of the feeling that General Milosevic could make decisions of his own without any approval from the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. Just one question for clarification. When you say that the intersections were targeted, who was frequenting these intersections?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, people who had cars began working in Sarajevo. Those more courageous among them used those cars to leave Dobrinja to go to work, and sometimes you would have traffic jams on certain intersections and then such intersections would be shelled. Another example would be the bus line established in 1995 so as to try and loosen up the situation psychologically, to do with the away with the fear of the siege, and then they targeted buses. And another example was the blue road which opened in 1995. If there was a convoy of importance trying to enter Dobrinja, it would encounter artillery, and it would stop the convoy or destroy the cargo as they were trying to get into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one other follow up question. Who was in this convoy that tried to enter Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the blue road was open, or the blue roads, most convoys were from the civilian sector organised by either the executive or the civilian protection, and those convoys were supposed to bring firewood, food, anything needed by the Sarajevo inhabitants the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It also included oil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President. I just have one final question for clarification on Exhibit P333, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you marked that building in red which comprises your brigade headquarters; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I think you also said that on this building, on this photo, you cannot see the actual headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you just marked the whole building as, you know, the building in which your headquarter was located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there other people living at that time in the house?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my family included.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination-in-chief. I think it took me about two and a half hours, which includes Your Honours' questions. I have no problem with that. I'm guilty because I overstepped the initial time-period, but just to let Your Honours know that it with would be great if we could complete with cross-examination of this witness today, for various reasons, one includes the health of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I shall try not to worsen your health condition, but there is one question that I would like you to clarify a bit more, and that is -- that relates to your account of changes that occurred in Dobrinja when General Milosevic took power in Sarajevo in August 1994. My impression was, after having heard your answer to the Prosecutor's question, that seen from a civilian point of view, the situation actually worsened in Dobrinja after August 1994 in the sense that the attacks were -- became more frequent and became more comprehensive. I want you to tell me if is that correct understanding of the changes that occurred after August 1994, if any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your concern about my health. If you allow me, I would like to tell you that my blood sugar level is 14.4, but I will try to do my best. It is true that the situation deteriorated in a certain way, from the psychological point of view. One can already see peace coming on the horizon. We knew that the Serbian army cannot conquer us or enslave us or -- and that something like Srebrenica and Zepa could not be repeated. Upon the arrival of General Milosevic, the liberation action started on Mount Igman and Trebevic plateau, and our army was rather successful in that. However, any loss of territory resulted in punishment of civilians in Dobrinja and elsewhere, and I think that would be the most appropriate answer that I can give to your question. And if you allow me to say one more thing that was just remembered. That was the period when there was tactical gain played by the politicians and the military leadership in view of the forthcoming negotiations. According to some intelligence we had, the Serbian forces, in 1995, had a serious intention of entering the airport and capturing it, irrespective of the fact that UN forces were deployed there. Everybody says in the world that whoever takes possession of an airport actually controls the whole state, so that was an additional element in response to your answer. And thank God that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. When were Mount Igman and the other mountain liberated exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The offensive was launched sometime in mid-1994 and lasted until almost the end of 1995, July or August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Interpretation] You know that the nature of cross-examination is such that I have to take into consideration the health condition of the witness; but at the same time, I cannot refrain from asking certain questions that are inevitable. My learned colleague Mr. Waespi perhaps could have curtailed his examination, and I will do my best to do so as much as possible. However, I have a whole bunch of documents that, in my view, are self-explanatory, and I will have to speak certain explanations from the witness. This is, of course, all going to be under your supervision, and it will be up to you to decide when I should conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic, and I have a number of questions for you, and I would like some clarifications from you. His Honour Judge Mindua, I think, asked you something about military police. Is it true that before you took over in July 1992, the command of your brigade, which operated in Dobrinja, that in those months preceding July, you spent as a member of a military police unit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the process of self-organisation and the creation of these voluntary units, I joined a group of men who were in sports; in other words, these men were both patriots and sportsmen. In -- in order for them to be able to communicate, we went to the Ministry of Defence and asked them to register us as voluntary unit, and Mr. Efendic, the then commander of the Territorial Defence, and Minister of Defence Djuko issued a decision granting us the status of military police; and in terms of being recognised as such, we were given 30 credentials of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were armed with whatever was available at the time. A few automatic rifles, pistols, and M56 Yugoslav automatic rifles, the Russian drum cartridge, but very few were able to purchase something or acquire something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, on the 4th of March at 1429, I received a document from the Prosecution and I marked it as DD00-01265. Once you see this document on your monitor, I would like to ask you a few questions. The Committee for Collecting Information on Crime Committed against Humanity and International Law, from January 1998 compiled in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document be put up, in order for the witness to answer a few questions. The document has been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If can you see this, this document was drafted in Belgrade by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I would like to draw your attention to that fact, and this document was disclosed by the Prosecution. Can you see this document, and can you confirm that I read the cover page correctly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just said that this was a document that came from Belgrade, from an institution in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that it was a Committee for Compiling Data on Crimes against Humanity and International Law. That's also what I said?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be useful to know under whose auspices this committee did its work. If they were appointed by a particular body, what body was that? Does the document itself tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can give you an answer immediately, and I think you will find it interesting. This is document was draft in 1998 by a committee set up at the time when Slobodan Milosevic was president of state. I received this document from the Prosecution, and I would like to present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the information that I requested? Is it contained in the document, or are you providing it to me on your own?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I received this from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You say so, but you're the person presenting it, not the Prosecution, so you should be prepared. If you're going to relying on this document, we need to know its antecedents. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can shed light on the source of this document. We received it from the Defence the General Galic. All the ERN numbers that have a Y at the beginning are documents that were given during the Galic case to the Prosecution, and this document has been made available to the Defence of Dragomir Milosevic ages ago, because they received all disclosure in the Galic case. I just saw it over the weekend again, and I showed it to the witness. And I gave it to Defence again because I knew that was the document the Defence is interested in. So I don't know about what this document is about. The Defence in Galic was providing it to us. That's all I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Serbian front page seems to reveal that the document was prepared by something called the Patriotic League. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, the state of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia set up a state committee For compiling data on crimes against humanitarian and international law; therefore, this committee was an official body of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this is an official document. I have would probably not have used it had I not received it a couple of days ago from the Prosecution; but in view of some other information, I think it can be used as an introduction into cross-examination of Mr. Hadzic. So this is an official document produced by the committee of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia related to various crimes and persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume that you were also questioned there; but given that we are looking at this document now, can we move to page 8 in B/C/S and also page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at item 3, "Participation of Muslim armed formations in committing the crimes against Serbs of Sarajevo during the war." Can you see that? Can you see that item, that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read the first two paragraphs to you: "At the time of the beginning of the war, Muslims and Croats in Sarajevo were ready for a war and the forthcoming mass crimes against the Serbs. The police forces had been almost entirely cleansed of Serbs, especially at the management level, and the illegal military units within the Patriotic League, Green Berets, and others had been reinforced. Within the Territorial Defence and reserve police, there had also been some independent arm the units, which perpetrated mass crimes against Serbs since the beginning of the war." My question is: Were your police forces that you were a member of involved in the commission of these kind of crimes?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I go back to the document that we're looking at it? It is interesting, Mr. Tapuskovic, to look at the year when this document was drafted. That's 1998. It is also interesting that it came from Belgrade, and I am familiar with this document. I saw it on the internet, but interestingly, both this document and this committee had been set up after the ICTY had been established and indictments issued against Serbs for the crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia. Therefore, since Serbia is the country with a rule of law, I suppose that certain people were tasked with preparing this kind of document as a kind of response or to put up accusations against people who did nothing. As for my unit, which was composed of 30 men, did only honourable work in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at paragraph 2, the last sentence of paragraph 2, which reads --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We cannot see it on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, just a minute. The English is not on the screen; and since you're reading it, it's helpful to the interpreters to have it on the screen. May we have the English on the screen. It's there now. Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 2, Mr. Hadzic: "And Serbs were killed and tortured both during the forced trench and tunnel digging and in other places and particularly under the Trebevic mountain." Do you know anything about this since you were a member of this unit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were not being killed or tortured in Dobrinja; neither were they digging the tunnel that you mention. There were Serbs, though, in the civilian protection who were digging these communication trenches, but they were not killed. They were treated as other residents of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, assuming that this statement in the report is true, and that Serbs were in fact tortured in Dobrinja in the tunnel killing, how would that affect the charges that the accused must answer? In other words, how does it affect the criminal liability of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can explain that, and we shall come back to that issue many times during this trial. The Serbs were defending themselves in the places where they lived, particularly to avoid what was happening to them in 1992. And the whole point of this conflict, as far as they were concerned, was to save their dear lives and to avoid what was happening in 1992. That was probably their primary reason. That was a paranoic fear of what happened in 1992, and we shall demonstrate that was the underlying motive of all their actions, in addition to political and other reasons as well that permeated this conflict. In the next passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that whatever actions the Serbs took were essentially of a defensive character?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and particularly at the time that the relevant time that we're discussing when they were much weaker, even in terms of the quantity of weapons they possessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, always remember if you introduce evidence, it must relevant. It must be evidence that relates to the charges in the indictment and, in particular, evidence that relates to the criminal liability of the accused in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is mention in the third paragraph of the people who spearheaded these actions, including and also --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
