utterances.text: But, first of all, I would like Mr. Hadzic to tell me if he took part in all that at the time.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, your statement that the Serbs were engaged is not true. In Sarajevo, whenever the Serbs were unable to keep these territories following the political instructions that they received, they preferred to leave Sarajevo. The only Serbs who remained behind were the ones who loved Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at page 12 now. Can you first tell me: During the whole war, including the relevant period, were there over 100 camps in the Territorial Defence of Sarajevo where Serbs were detained and taken away to be executed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, but I claim that there were no camps in Sarajevo. There were no camps in Sarajevo as far as I could deduce from the footage shown on TV. There were only camps run by Serbs, but there were no camps in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 12 of this report, item 3.2, which mentions you. Item 3.7 mentions your name, and it also mentions Dobrinja. It reads: "In this suburb, the prison was based in the Baltazar cafe held by the members of Dragan Vikic's unit. There's also mention of Stela, and it says that you were very close to Alija Izetbegovic. However, there were also camps, Poljoo Prema cellar, garages, and all the rest of that was under your control. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me which period are we talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Including the period when you were in the police, and the relevant period that we're discussing here today.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, these allegations here are not true. I know that before the war there was a Baltazar cafe, highly reputed cafe. It was close to the police administration building, but I don't know that there was ever a camp there. Next thing, I don't think anything about Stela camp in Dobrinja. There was a Stela camp in Vogosca, and I know that this is where the Serbs imprisoned Bosniaks. And the third allegation, which says Hadzic was also in very close contact with Alija Izetbegovic, I can say that I am proud to have known our late president; and through my contacts and associations with him, I only became a better person. I could only learn good things, not evil things from him, and I am very happy to have known him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your relationship with Mr. Izetbegovic. How did that come about and what form did it take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To cut it short, I met Mr. Izetbegovic before the war. We were not close friends; acquaintances rather. During the first democratic election, I assisted his party to win, in a way. And President Izetbegovic held that in high regard. After that, he offered me a position within the executive, but I refused. I told I have a good job, and I have no need to get into all that. This is how old our friendship was. He also expressed his concern during the time when the situation in Dobrinja was the worst, and when it was psychologically the most difficult for the population. At that time, he came at Dobrinja telling people to try and stay there and not to leave, and I will never forget that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing concerning this document, you don't even know of the camp called Sunce, the Sun. It was under your direct control. You don't know of that either?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, as I said when testifying in the Galic case, I knew of -- of something else which was called Granap Sunce, the Sun. I don't know of any camp of such name. There was a detention for the members of the Territorial Defence, but I don't know who was held there. We were not part of that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But there was a detention centre there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military formation. The Territorial Defence had an independent battalion within which it had its own detention for soldiers, those who tried to cross the runway; who smuggled; those who got drunk or acted the against the rules of service or the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing. Just below where it is mentioned that were in close contact with Milosevic, under 3-8, it say, Himzo Cesko, who was a policeman before the war in Sarajevo, had his own sniping team targeting Serbian civilians from high-rises in Sarajevo, such as the Elektroprivreda, the Hotel Bristol, and other buildings. Are you familiar with that, even outside the scope of the relevant time that we're discussing now?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it ridiculous that you ask that question. I was in Dobrinja. We were under siege, and I don't know of many things in the city, and I don't know this person mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at least hear about the tactics they employed, that those policemen with the assistance of the MUP assumed positions in those high-rises, and then snipers were advised as to the location of Serb civilians, so as to target them. That would take place after such civilians would go through a checkpoint, and then it would be radioed to the snipers to target them?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to tender this document, being DD00-01265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D104.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I respect your position concerning this document since it originated from the FRY, and I'm not trying to put here that it was proven. However, is there a proceedings against you before the cantonal court in Sarajevo, a biforked [as interpreted] proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, during the last elections, I was on the federal list of candidates for a deputy. The court provided their approval for each and every person on the list. Had there been any proceedings instituted against me, my name could not have been there. I don't know of any investigations or proceedings before either the cantonal or any other court, which is confirmed by the example I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to place your name on the federal electoral list, you have to provide a certificate by the cantonal court, where now its proceedings are taking place against you and that you have no previous criminal record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in the question that you asked something has been translated as a "biforked proceeding." "Biforked proceedings." What is it that you have in mind here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two separate criminal proceedings against Mr. Hadzic. I was imprecise or rather the interpretation was erroneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I never understood politics; hence, I'm asking you directly. A document under the number KT 326 from 2006. In any case, it is KT 326/95. Although, that may be incorrect. In any case, is there an investigation or proceedings against you for a murder of a Bosniak by the name of Rajif Kordic? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it, and I hear it from you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is there an investigation against you for the murder of 15 Muslims? Was there a criminal report submitted for that crime claiming that you participated in their killing; whereas, it was portrayed as if the Serbs killed them. One of the people involved was Rajif Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a proceedings against you for the murder of 30 Serbian inhabitants who were killed digging trenches, as was stated in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, or rather, I don't know about it. I guess the court would have let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have another piece of information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in relation to all these questions, which are so specific as they relate to legal proceedings against the accused, do you have at hand the various court documents with these charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received that information a few days ago, and I will certainly forward it to the Bench. These are court documents, these being criminal records or investigations or criminal reports. I don't have them right now, but I will be in a position to hand them over. I just wanted to ask the witness whether he is familiar with any of it. Just one more thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, before you say one more thing, I will say that I will take a very dim view of what you have done in putting these allegations to the witness if you don't have supporting documents. I see this as different from the usual case where a Defence counsel will put to a witness a certain point of view on the basis of instructions that he has. And in presenting his case, in presenting the Defence case, the counsel will adduce that evidence. But what kind of weight would you expect us to attach to this line of questioning if you don't have that documentation to put to the witness? I will attach very little weight to it, and I take a very dim view of that kind of approach. So I expect you to produce the court documents with these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is very difficult to position oneself in a case like this. But in any case, I will have those documents. And although the witness will not be here anymore, I'm sure I am not mistaken. Since he was allowed to talk about rumours in the examination-in-chief, I think this should be allowed as well. These are not rumours. These are matters before the cantonal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is on an entirely different plane. These are serious allegations. This has nothing to do with a rumour. If you have been instructed as part of your Defence case that this witness has been charged by courts in this country with certain crimes, I would expect you to have the court documents verifying this. And I expected you to have it now, not in two or three days times when the witness is not here to address them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. I was trying to tell you that we have an investigation under way, but at the same time we are very limited in resources in terms of personnel. I see that you attach great importance to these documents, and later on I will try to introduce such documents through another witness, if I may. I just wanted to put another thing before the witness, and I am sure he knows something about that. It has to do with a magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I do attach importance to it because counsel has a responsibility to follow certain ethical standards in presenting his case. Responsible counsel doesn't simply put allegations to a witness that he cannot back up. It's not as though you will present this evidence when you present the case for the accused. That I understand. But I see this as being different. You're saying you're told that this gentleman has been charged in his country with particular offences. You must show him the charges. It's not sufficient merely to -- to say that you have been informed. That's not the action of responsible counsel. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept everything you said. You're completely right. But from this moment on, I will rely solely on documents and nothing else. According to the information received from Mr. Waespi on the 4th of March, there is a statement given to the OTP. It is document DD00-1263, and I would like to put it to the witness for comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see the document. Somewhere in the middle you talked about your area of responsibility. You also said something you said a minute ago. The witness noticed that General Milosevic was more subtle when choosing targets of shelling and sniping activity. There was another thing you said about snipers, and I want the to show you another document that has been marked for identification. The number was D990682. And before the end of my cross-examination, I will go back to the snipers many a time. However, you told us you had no snipers. This is an order by General Legit Idodjic [phoen], dated the 14th of February, whereby he says that "due to the technical need of the unit in order for them to carry out combat activities in full, I record that all brigades are to secure" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you have a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think the witness said they we didn't have snipers. We discussed at the length that sniping rifles that were used. Maybe it is a different term. Maybe they're called sometimes marksmen, but I don't recall that the witness said that they didn't have snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is strictly correct, Mr. Tapuskovic. The witness testified that they didn't have as sophisticated weapons as the other side did, but he never said that they didn't have snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with that. I was imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What you said has to do with the document. In the document, it states that "all brigades are to secure the hand over and transport of three sniping rifles to the warehouse department of the 1st Corps. That means all brigades. "Secondly, the aforementioned weaponry need to be fully operational, and unit commanders are to notify me in person as to implementation of tasks." These are sniping rifles which are in full operational order ready to be used. In that regard, this does not tally with what the witness said. My question is: Does he know of this order and whether his brigade received such sniping rifles?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you've read it out yourself. The command of the corps demanded the brigade to hand over sniping rifles if they had any. Do you have a document that would state that we indeed handed them over? This is what the corps command asked from all the brigades to hand over sniping rifles. Where did we hand them over, or who did we hand it over to, those modern sniping rifles as you say? Maybe in order to fulfil this order, we took three hunting rifles with binoculars and handed them over, although I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a translation to this document; if not, may I just ask the interpreter to translate number 1 and number 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "I hereby order, under 1, all brigades are to secure the hand over and transport of three sniping rifles to the warehouse department of LOB," Interpreter's note: we don't know what the abbreviation is, "of the 1st Corps-Krupa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it say "of three sniping rifles." The hand over and transport of three sniping rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of three sniping rifles each. My colleague is telling me that the "LOB" means logistics base. Mr. Tapuskovic, just said "each of the brigades."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am sorry. Can you read it again to me. I'm a little puzzled by the very specific reference to "three sniping rifles."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "All brigades are to secure the hand over and transport of three sniping rifles each to the warehouse department of the logistics base of the 1st Corps-Krupa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What does number 2 say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The aforementioned weaponry needs to be fully operational, and the unit commanders are to report to me personally as to the implementation of tasks. Deadline: The 17th of February, 1994, 2400 hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, number 1, the interpretation that we received would seem to suggest that the -- the author of this order believed that there existed three sniping rifles and that he was requiring that these be handed over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I don't think you understood item 1 properly. In this order, it is stated that "all brigades are to hand over three sniping rifles each to the corps command." It would be exceptionally clear and most interesting to see another document to go with this commander. That document should testify about the implementation of this order so as to see what weaponry was handed over to the 1st Corps by each of the brigades. Here we have nine brigades mentioned. It should have amounted to a total of about 30 rifles if they had any. Had they -- if they had any, they were supposed to hand them over to the 1st Corps for their perusal. That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why three sniping rifles each? Why not just any sniping rifles? Hand over any and all sniping rifles that are in your possession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment about the number 3. I don't know why the staff commander mentioned three and not something else. It is quite clear to me that he himself didn't know what each of the brigades had and what type of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you said that under your brigade, no such rifles were delivered to the 1st Corps because you did not have any such weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I did not say we did not hand over any, but we may have provided the next closest thing. It could have been a hunting rifle or a carbine with an optical sight that might have met the needs of this order. I didn't see we didn't hand over any. I simply don't know. If we could see a follow-up to this document, an overview of what was handed over by the brigades and what type of weaponry was handed over, then we would be able to establish if indeed we handed over anything and what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer is very interesting, because it seems to me that you are interpreting the order to imply that this was an attempt to reallocate sniping rifles from the brigades to the 1st Corps. So it was merely a question of bringing some weapons in from the brigades to the 1st Corps where these weapons were needed. Is that a correct understanding of your interpretation of this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Probably the corps command needed these weapons for some activity that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, item 2 does not speak about ordinary weapons, but it says that "the above mentioned weapons must be fully operational, and unit commanders shall report to me personally about the implementation of the task." According to this order, it means that these snipers were supposed to be in perfect working order?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the order specified that PSPs and the Argentinean rifles were to be handed over, then I would understand it. But as I understand and read this, this could have applied to virtually anything. You could hand over whatever you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what you say, but the order reads differently, and it says "in perfect working order."

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hunting rifle, a hunting sniper can also be in perfect working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Zrak factory that you mentioned, did it manufacture throughout the war primarily sniper rifles and optical devices for the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably you should have more information about this than I do. As far as I know, Zrak manufactured only optical devices because only some of them -- the machines and workforce remained there. The rest of them went away or joined the army. Only a few people remained working there, and the factory was virtually closed down. They could have probably did some repair work on optical devices; however, there were no technical possibilities or capacity for the Zrak to manufacture any weapons during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back now to this information. In addition to what you said about sniping, you also said that -- that under the control of Dragomir Milosevic, the activities were more subtle and more precise and more -- and definitely more dangerous than during the time of General Galic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: By that you imply and include also the incident when the Simone Bolivar school was hit and the TV building as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also include here the incidents when a sniper killed two or three people with one shot.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would only make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this exhibit DD00-1263 into evidence as Defence Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also DD00- -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please give that a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently, it's an MFI so we can now admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D99 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the old MFI number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The old MFI was MFI 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you have another one, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is 0682?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an entirely different document. It's DD00-1263, the information provided by the Prosecution. It's an entirely different document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I proceed with other documents, I would like to address the statement made by this witness of 24th and 25th of October. It's DD00-1083. Let's start from page 7 of -- oh, no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement? There's a signature on the left?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's start from bullet paragraph relating to the defence tactics of the Dobrinja Brigade, and that's on page 7. It starts by you saying that you read a number of books, military books, and that you also read about the biography of General Kutusov?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except General Kutusov.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you also made reference to Churchill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I had to read these books in order to upgrade my military knowledge. We found a book written by Mr. Churchill about how the British defended London during World War II, and this set up of survival for London we copied and applied it in Dobrinja in order for to us to survive as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever study anything to do with the military organisation of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any need to do that because I had trained officers on my staff who were able to provide this expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from these officers you received certain information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just made certain propositions and proposals. If I found them to be sensible and reasonable, I accept them. If not, I wouldn't accept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the matters contained in the instruction on working maps how certain placement of artillery and other weapons are to be marked within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not interested in those kind of markings. I was only interested in survival and maintaining life. There were shortages of gas and everything else. We had to find a way to defend ourselves and how to bring all these 27.000 people until the end of the war, and to protect them from genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your working military maps, how did you mark certain positions of yours? Both firing position and command position.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I can see a map, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me this about the mountain brigade: You said that a mountain brigade is something named in that way or described in that way according to the number of troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that as far as I know, a mountain brigade, on paper, is a brigade that should, as per establishment, have a certain number of men and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go up to Mojmilo hill where you held positions? Were you a mountain brigade at that time as well, because you were on a hill and that's why you were called a mountain brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true. As a brigade we never went up the Mojmilo hill, but we, rather, in 1992, cut off Mojmilo and closed the circle in order to prevent the Serbian forces of penetrating our area. By the way, a mountain brigade is not called after a mountain or a hill. It has its name according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that at the relevant period, when Dragomir Milosevic was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, a part of Mojmilo was under your control and the other part of Mojmilo was under the control of Dragomir Milosevic and his troops.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that a part of Mojmilo was no-man's land- that was on the left-hand side where the water reservoir was- until that time when, in 1995, we connected trenches with the 101st Brigade and closed the circle. The right-hand side of Mojmilo was under the control of Mr. Milosevic as far as Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, both the VRS was on Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has its lines on the peaks of the hills that were under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are saying that they were not at the foot of the hill.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were always on the other side. At the foot of the hill there is one of the barracks in Lukavica. Serbian forces had held the Mojmilo hill, and at the foot of it, there was the former JNA barracks in Lukavica, one of the two that they had there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, that this barracks was completely below or at the foot of Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you want to hear from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have heard enough. Let us go back to the statement, and I have to read a part concerning the defensive tactics of Dobrinja Brigade. At page 7, paragraph 3, you say as follows: "Using the British manuals as a guide, we constructed trenches 2 metres deep all around the perimeter of Dobrinja, except the portion facing the airport. The trenches were built with a fire step, with a protective firing position, a drainage channel, and were deep enough to protect the soldiers from view and direct fire." And at the end you say that the trenches were sandbagged and riveted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is correct except that we didn't have sand and we didn't reinforce them with stone but rather with -- we put slabs at the bottom of trenches to make walking easier. Dobrinja, geographically speaking, is a water source area. Every 1.5 or 2 metres deep you run into water. Whenever you start digging a trench, after 1 or 2 metres, you discover water. And that was one of the reasons why we used this British warfare manual, where the British used to dig trenches in moors, and from that we learned how to drain the trenches. So at the elevation of 50 centimetres, we use the slabs, to place them there to facilitate walking, and to build the communication trenches. If we didn't do that, we would be constantly standing or walking in water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in this last sentence, which says: "The trenches were sandbagged and were reinforced with stone." You said you didn't have sand. How do you explain and account for this being stated in your statement? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no -- there was no sand lining of the trenches. However, the soldiers were protected with bags filled with all kinds of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the last paragraph on page 7, which says: "Company HQ were in buildings nearby in warm shelters so that they could retain command and control. A long trench was constructed starting on Mojmilo, zigzagging down the hill." Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long trench was constructed, zigzagging down the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no trench on Mojmilo. However, there is a natural depression resembling a trench where -- which could provide access to Mojmilo. However, a long trench was built on Mojmilo. It was -- it probably refers to the one dug out in 1995, which connected our two units, in order to prevent precipitation entering the trenches. And that is why we built it in a zigzag shape, as far as the position of the 101st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you now. First you said it's not correct; now you're saying it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just continue. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, you said there was no zigzag trench.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This zigzag trench was dug out in early 1995, at the same time when the blue road was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look a little bit down there, where you say that there were firing positions in buildings. In other words, you had firing positions in civilian facilitates.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, those buildings were abandoned and burned. There were no civilians there. On the edges of Dobrinja neighbourhood, all buildings were burned. There was no one living there. In Dobrinja 5 alone, 880 flats were destroyed. During the war, in the whole of Dobrinja, 3.000 flats were destroyed and 2.000 were rendered uninhabitable. All these buildings on the edges of the suburb were shelled and destroyed, and there was no one else staying there apart from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did have firing positions that were situated in civilian residential areas.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you listened or looked carefully on the map of our trenches, you could have seen that they followed natural configuration of the terrain, avoiding all residential buildings. If it ran into a building, we had to maintain this line, but these buildings were vacated. That is where we put our guards in order to prevent the Serbian forces from coming in. What did you except us to do? That we did not have soldiers in those buildings, that would be gaps in our defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying the same as you are; that it is true that you had your firing positions in these buildings.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the abandoned buildings, and I think that's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How about the roofs of the buildings? Did you have camouflaged weapons? And I'm referring to your HQ building.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of roof are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just say what kind of roof you are referring to and then we'll stop. And just before the break, I'll give a decision on a Prosecution motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the building near the Simone Bolivar school where their command post was. On the roof of that building, or inside the building, were there any weapons and firing positions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no weapons or firing positions in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll stop here for the moment, and I'll now give an a decision on the Prosecution motion filed on the 20th of February for the admission of written witness statements of five witnesses, including Rupert Smith, pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Defence takes no position on the motion but requests that it be allocated reasonable time for cross-examination. The Chamber will only address the Prosecution's request for the admission of Mr. Smith's statement. We'll give a decision on the other witnesses at a later date. The Chamber grants the Prosecution motion, admits the witness statement of Rupert Smith into evidence upon fulfilment of the conditions set out in Rule 92 ter. The time originally estimated for this witness's testimony by the Prosecution was five hours. The Chamber notes, however, that in its motion, the Prosecution estimates that the overall length of time required is two and a half hours. The Chamber notes the significance of the testimony of the witness and that the Prosecution intends to refer to 21 exhibits during the testimony of this witness. In the result, the Chamber will allocate one hour and a half to the Prosecution for examination-in-chief and three hours to the Defence for cross-examination. We'll now take the break

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I obviously don't want to, you know, kind of negatively to refer to your decision to allocate time; but just to reiterate that, it is important that this witness finishes today. And in relation to General Smith, equally, we hope that we can finish him tomorrow morning. I can tell that you examination-in-chief will be less than we had originally planned with General Smith. It will be around an hour, hour and 15 minutes, and it will be around half the documents that you mentioned, so around ten documents. So, again, we hope that we can finish with this witness today, and tomorrow's witness tomorrow. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there is something that may run contrary to that, because have I been informed that the Victims and Witness Protection Unit has expressed some concern about the health of the witness. So, Mr. Hadzic -- Witness, I'm addressing you. I understand that you may be having some problems with your health. You referred to your blood sugar, and I understand that it may be very high. And I am to let you know that if you wish to have a break, all you do have do is request it and I will grant it, because your health obviously comes first. Do you understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that my blood sugar levels are high, but I will try to get through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to respect that a person is either capable of incapable of testifying. We were warned of that before this witness started testifying, and I would have excepted that Mr. Waespi would have paid attention to that as well. I, on my part, will do my best to respect that; but if the witness is unable to continue, of course, I have to abide by it. We can pause at any moment, but some things must be discussed here before you. I will try to pose my questions the way that the witness, if possible, could answer with a mere yes or no. That's what I will try to do, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So as not to dwell on the topic that we discussed before the break any longer, in your statement on page 11, you speak of the tunnel which was dug under the airport runway. That is page 11, and I believe in the English it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 11. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this chapter about the creation and use of the Dobrinja-Butmir tunnel, we can look at the first sentence. You say that you had a cannon, no, rather a tank up there at Zuc. Is it correct that it remained at Zuc throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that there was a tank, but it wasn't at Zuc throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It changed position?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where it was, but it was located at the Jusuf Dzonlic barracks. That's where it under went maintenance. It was rather damaged since it was pulled down from Mojmilo hill; and when Zuc was being defended, it was put up there. But due to inability to operate it properly, it was hit that bay by a Maljutka rocket and rendered inoperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood probably, you said when there was an offensive, and here it says that there was defence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time there was combat at Zuc. The Serb forces were at the outskirts of the settlement, at the foot of Zuc hill. Basically, throughout the war, the Bosnian army was trying to push the Serbian forces as from far away from the settlement as possible, so as to protect the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the tunnel, if things were as stated here, perhaps you can tell me the following, and you can say, yes or no. I will read out the fourth paragraph: "The tunnel was officially opened on 30th of July 1993, after three months of digging. It had been dug through a very waterlogged area which should have been impossible. It was improved as time wept by with the installation of rail tracks, timber revetting, telephone communications to either end, and eventually fuel pipes and a six-kilowatt electricity capable. The tunnel was 860 metres long and had been dug by hand in shifts." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Until December 1993, we were in charge of the Dobrinja end of the tunnel, and the 4th Brigade was in charge of the Butmir end. After that, the 1st Corps took over control of the tunnel. I don't think the enemy every found out exactly where the tunnel entrance was. At the Dobrinja end, there were two entrances in adjacent garages. One was for the railed section, which went under the garage, through a trench under the road, and to the actual tunnel entrance in a house near the airport. The other one was for people on foot." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the final version of the tunnel, and that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I have in mind the times between the 10th of August, 1994 until the 31st of November, 1995, because that is the time material for the indictment of Dragomir Milosevic and that was the time during which he held his function.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can discuss a military matter now. Your brigade was a part of the 12th Division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The entire 12th Division was in Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had three divisions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 14th Division had its location in Tarcin, in the area of Igman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their command post was in Tarcin and their area of responsibility was Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 16th Division was in Vares, Nisici, Breza, Visocor, up to Kobilica Vaya Kiskodec [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that the 1st Corps comprised those three divisions; the 12th, the 14th, and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I finally received a translation. It is a Defence document DD00-0121. It is a report on the situation of the 1st Corps and the other corps, and the document stems from the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This has been translated, and I kindly ask for the document to be brought on screen, so that I can ask the witness a few things about it. It is DD00-0121. It seems we have another problem with e-court. This is my most important document, and I put it in two days ago. It has a translation into English. I can show it to you. It has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, have a look. I have such documents for each month, but this one is for the 24th of August, 1994 by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina signed by the chief of administration, Hadim Majbregolic [phoen]. It is the personnel section and the section for legal affairs. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see what it says. Based on the orders -- pursuant to the order of the RBH OSSVK, strictly confidential, dated the 5th of February, 1994. "We hereby send you a report on manning levels as at 1 August 1994." Have I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your knowledge, is that the time when Dragomir Milosevic took over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the exact date. You are probably more away of it than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here "manning levels of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 1 August 1994. Was this followed? The SVK with headquarters support units, 1639, the 1st Corps, 62.899 fighters." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps over 63.000; The 3rd Corps, 35; the 4th Corps, and son on and so forth. Total 227.256. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo and around Sarajevo in the three divisions, there were 62.000 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the documents states.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And we have the age breakdown; younger than 35, 135.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 36 and 40, 37.000; between 41 and 45, 23.000; and over 45, as many as 19.640. There were women, six and a half thousand. If it is as stated in the document, it means that the 1st Corps was the most numerous. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps had more according to the data shown; 63.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Out of the 62.000, in Sarajevo itself, there were over 40.000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Together with the police, there were around 60.000 armed people. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not armed. The figure was 60.000, but we don't know about the arms. I don't think 100 per cent of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are trying to tell us that while Dragomir Milosevic was in command not all 62.000 were armed.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that my brigade was never fully armed. We always had more men than arms. There was always a certain percentage, a degree of people being armed in the corps; and probably in the corps, you can find the documents showing the exact percentage of the people armed; the statistical data about the manning levels of the Bosnia-Herzegovina corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me at least whether at the time of the offensive in June, there were still people who participated in the offensive without any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which offensive do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Igman-Trebevica plateau? At all front lines. You have to be specific line. You have to tell me which offensive. I cannot respond to an open-ended question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am getting there. I have five such orders, but I'm interested in the offensive that began on the 5th of June and ended somewhat later that year. Was there a single person participating in the offensive without a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm asking you, again. Was that the offensive called the deblocking of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just an admonition that there are pauses made between the questions an answers, and if the English translation could be shown, the complete English translation. Because there is on the B/C/S version a paragraph at the end above the signature block, and I'd like to see that in English. And just for Your Honours understanding, this is the first time that I see this document and certainly an English translation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please observe, Witness and Mr. Tapuskovic, a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have an opportunity to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, I had the offensive called offensive T or Tekbir in mind, Mr. Hadzic. We had the 3rd and the 7th Corps participating in that one, not only the first one, the 1st Corps, but also the 3rd and the 7th with all of their troops participating in that June offensive. That is the offensive I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the offensive that you are mentioning, Tekbir, I don't know that it was called that. I know it was called offensive for lifting the blockade of the city of Sarajevo; and it is true that in this attempt to lift the blockade from the city of Sarajevo, all corps of the BH army took place. And for your information, I would like to tell that this offensive failed. Our forces were defeated and the blockade remained -- of Sarajevo remained in place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it is not disputable that the total numerical strength of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was 18.000?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, that's what you say. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what the indictment says. These men who were in Sarajevo-Romanija Corps managed to defend themselves from nearly 200.000 men who were attacking Sarajevo, and the 80.000 managed to defend themselves. How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's theory, and you have based your question on that. According to establishment, how many men should a corps have, 18.000 or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document, DD00-0121, be tendered as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't have an objection to the document being tendered. But just an observation: On page 74, line 3/4 of the transcript, the Defence asked the question that "Together with the police there were about 60.000 armed people." And I don't see any mentioning to the police in this document. I just received -- I just read now the whole English line. So I didn't know what the issue was about these 60.000 people having included the police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my question and he gave the answer that he gave. I didn't relate it to this document. I'm talking about the police. I will go back to this document later, and the number is DD00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I don't find any objection to the question since it wasn't specifically related to the document. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have document DD00-1121 admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like now to show the witness a number of documents relating to the functioning of a facility named D-B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this annotation was used by the 1st Corps of the BH army for the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. DB stands for Dobrinja-Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us first look at an order dated 13 April 1995 relating to the operation of this tunnel. That's document DD00-0751, produced by the BH army, by Mr. Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can see this document. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, was Mr. Prevljak the commander of the 12th Division in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This order has been even sent to your brigade, 155th, and it very specifically stipulates by the hour how this facility should be operated. If you look at page 1 first, does it say here that as a result of the fact that certain changes took place in the mode of operation of DB facility, and for the purpose of a more operational work, certain ties were specified for the usage of this facility? And that is to do with giving -- allotting times for those given permission to pass through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I take it there is no translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is the translation, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have been waiting for the translation since the 9th of March, but I don't have it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The 9th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. We were told that we would receive it on the 9th of March. That's what my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was it submitted for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the first documents. I don't know the exact date, when I submitted over 100 documents. We were told that it should be completed by the 9th of March, the translation, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two pages, one sentence, in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Identify the passages that you wish to refer to, and we'll rely on the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I need is for the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the point that you're making about the tunnel? What's the point of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here very precisely, during the day, who is allowed to pass at 6.00 a.m., at 8.00 a.m., at 10.00 a.m., 11.00 a.m., so that's the schedule of the use of the tunnel by the hour, or, in other words, this is an hourly schedule of the usage of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But what consequences flow from that so far as this trial is concerned? Because it's not in dispute that the tunnel was there and it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is exactly what I intend to demonstrate, that certain orders were issued, giving permission for units to pass through the tunnel and become engaged in operations outside the Sarajevo zone. I have a number of important documents showing how all this was functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But to be relevant to the proceedings, you have to go a little further, in my view, to show not just that they passed through the tunnel and were engaged in operations outside the Sarajevo zone, but that those operations in which they were engaged were of a defensive character; that they were responding to attacks from the other side, and that the consequence for this trial is that those charges in the indictment which relate to that particular incident, the accused is not responsible for them. Otherwise, it's not leading anywhere, merely to show that the Bosnian government forces engaged in attacks. You have to tie it to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly what I intended to do, and I can produce at least 100 documents to this effect; however, chose only four. And this document, DD00-01170, directly relates to your question. If we can have it displayed on our screens please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it says here, "The command of the 12th division, strictly confidential --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please indicate where he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, the interpreter is asking you, and so are we, to indicate where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 1, the heading, the very top of the document. "12th Division Command, strictly confidential, number" so-and-so, "Sarajevo, 26th of June, 1995." Is that what it says here.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Proposal for selected targets for destruction and engagement of aggressor forces." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Pursuant to order of the Chief of Staff of the 1st Corps, strictly confidential, number 01/3-151, dated 25th of June, 1995. For pursuant to active combat operations in areas of responsibility of all brigades and in the area of responsibility of the 12th Division with a view to engaging aggressor forces around the city and stretching them and releasing the burden on our forces outside of the city in the area of responsibility of the 14th and 16th Division, this is our proposal per brigade in its entirety." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the following: Does this mean that this order relating to specific actions aimed at attracting the aggressor to be carried out in the area of responsibility of the 12th and 16th Division?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't see what is disputable here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you. Look at page 3 of this document. It refers to your specific activities, of your 155th Brigade. That's page 3 of this document. Other brigade -- all other brigades are mentioned before your brigade. Look at this one here. It says, "155th Brigade." So it says here: "In the area of responsibility of the 155th Mountain Brigade, six targets are to be destroyed, two by each battalion, as follows: The house Ledica [phoen] in Nedzarici. The group should be composed of the gunner, the sniper shooter, two automatic operators, and a PAM which is anti-aircraft machine-gun operator assistant gunner." Does this imply that in this operation a sniper is to be involved in this operation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the order says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to carry out this order?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have the result of the compliance with this order, I can answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That would take too much time. I'm asking you did you receive this order.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but we never carried it out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel and witness should pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter is asking, again, for a pause between question and answer. But I wanted to ask the witness: Why was the order never carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the situation we were in, it was impossible to implement this order. The person writing it did not have any real idea of the situation in the field but, rather, it was a mere speculation of what we could do. We implemented a part of this order but the rest went unattended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a sniper shooter active in this operation as stated here?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, for the 100th time, in these areas of responsibility under my command, each soldier could be a sniper shooter in a way. Because in certain points at the separation line, the distance was as little as five metres or sometimes up to 50 at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I understand you then, you didn't have any soldiers who were specifically designated as snipers; but in implementing this order, you could identify two soldiers and they would effectively carry out the functions of a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why would the person ordering this state expressively that should a sniper shoot in addition to all the other troops, unless that person was counting on the fact that you had a proper sniper shooter and the piece of weaponry he would need?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to figure that out. What can I tell you in answer to your question, or rather, I would be able to answer your question if I were the person who wrote the order, but I'm not, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will refer you to some other orders, but this one, in other words, was supposed to be implemented so as to attract the attention of the soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; whereas, the real focus would in the area of responsibility of the 12th and the 14th -- no, sorry, the 16th corps, as stated in this order?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, it is correct. But an activity such this one, can they distract such a number of troops so as to enable an operation on the other end?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This order contains tasks for the 101st, next to you; for the 102th; for the 105th; the other three brigades; and for your brigade. You were to conduct four operations, each of which should be done with the help of a sniper shooter; in each of the four, a sniper shooter is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I provided an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was a full answer, too, and that's why I would kindly ask for DD00-1170 to be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D107, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that it be marked for identification until we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. We'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I forget, I would like to tender the statement, DD00-1083, and I propose it be made a Defence exhibit. Your Honours, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the witness statement dated the 24th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D107 will be marked for identification; and the latest document, DD00-1083, will become Exhibit D108.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also wanted to warn you of the following. The statement given by the witness on the 10th of July, 2006 is something we received a couple of days ago, and its translation as late as yesterday. Therefore, I had no opportunity to study that statement, and I don't think the witness was proofed on it as well. Therefore, I won't be able to pose any questions regarding that since I received it at such a late time, and I have no time to put it to -- before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the statement itself is in English, and it's only I think one or one and a half pages, a few paragraphs, has been disclosed, I guess, last year. But, indeed, yes, the translation was disclosed on Sunday, Sunday around 3.00 or 4.00. But it's a very short statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are 11 paragraphs, important ones. I will not make this an issue. I just wanted to give you a illustration of the situation we were in. It is an important issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you are not making it an issue, then so be it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is another order, DD00-1159, concerning the activities of the 155th Mountain Brigade. I think the number is correct, and it is already in front of witness. It is an order of the 13th of June, army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, command of the 12th Division. Order. Since the order of the 1st Corps command, strictly confidently, number 01/1-195 of the 2nd of June, 1995 was not fully complied with, being the preconditions of fulfilling combat tasks at Trebevica, we annul the order of the 13th of June and a new order follows in light of the facts mentioned. "I order that the command of the 152nd and 155th Mountain Brigade be sent to the Treskavica plateau, together with the necessary number of troops out of their unit, so that in the field there would be 300 soldiers in each. Number 2: In the manning structure, sent to carry out this task, you should take care that you have as many fighters as possible to fulfil the combat tasks issued." Mr. Hadzic, you implemented this ordered, didn't you? It was signed by Fikret Prevljak, the 12th Division commander.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did..

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to go through the tunnel in order to reach the positions mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a necessary thing to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the large map -- no, let me tender this one first, DD00-1159, and I propose it as a Defence exhibit. First of all, has this been admitted? DD00-1159 as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the court deputy enlighten us on that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it has not been admitted yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, again, similar situation like last time, we don't have any objections to have it admitted but we need a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes marked for identification D109.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you show us on this large map where the Treskavica positions were, where the tunnel is that you went there, and where did you go? It won't work. It seems that every time the witness is in front of the map, he doesn't want to see.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to hide. This is the runway, that's where the tunnel was, and we went up there to Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does the blue line depict? Are those the positions assumed by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be that. It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: In other words, in Sarajevo, you were setting up a smoke scene. You were causing incidents so as to avert attention from your real tasks which was going through the tunnel to some other areas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. In Sarajevo, we were defending ourselves trying to survive, and we went through the tunnel in order to liberate ourselves, to break free.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you went to any combat actions to the front lines depicted in blue.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether the combat activities in Sarajevo were merely a smoke screen so as to attract the attention of Serbian forces; whereas, we would then focus our operations outside of Sarajevo. To stress, yet again, in Sarajevo, we were trying to survive. There were no provocations. We were trying to defend ourselves from the aggressor. We went through the tunnel trying to breakthrough the siege and to try and drive them away, so that we could live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The document we saw a moment ago, in it you confirmed that those activities there were setting up a smoke screen, and that the focus of actions were outside on the units which left Sarajevo. That's what you told me; that's what you confirmed.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put it that way. I said that in addition to our regular defensive tasks, we were given some other tasks in order to lift the burden from the units outside, and those units were getting ready to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. Unfortunately, neither of us on the inside nor the units attempting to lift the blockade succeeded, and that is in no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in chief, you said that you spent almost nine months at Igman, and that your unit was more frequently outside than inside Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. That's not what I said. I said that the brigade was assigned an area of responsibility the size of a battalion, in order to defend the line at Igman, and such activities took place as of late 1993 until the Dayton Agreements. But it didn't include the entire brigade, only one of its battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you returned to Sarajevo to rest and then you went back to Igman; is that correct? And you went through the tunnel each time.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had shifts of 15 days, but what sort of a rest is it if you go back to Sarajevo, where there is constant shelling; and then after two days, you are returned to the front line again? Because during your absence, people were heavily burdened to try and cover up for the battalion which had been to pull out to Treskavica and to the plateau there. If you consider that to be a rest, well, to me, it's more of a torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of an order referring to sabotage action in which was counted only as provocation and smoke screen covering up actions elsewhere? Did you hear about these actions being taken both in Sarajevo and outside of Sarajevo for to you be enabled operate along this blue lines?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade was never involved in these kind of actions either inside or outside of Sarajevo. And I don't remember any other brigade being involved in that kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read out to you: Order, issued by your commander Fikret Prevljak on the 1st of July, 1995. That's document DD00-0741, and the translation of this order is due on the 9th of March, as we have been informed. So you can see this document here: The 12th Division command, the 1st of July, 1995, performance of attacks. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on to read as follows: "The experience acquired so far in conducting surprise attacks, both in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps and other corps, indicate the need and significance of carrying out sabotage actions against PZT. A very successfully -- a very well prepared surprise attack was carried out by units of the 2nd Corps inflicting significant losses on the aggressor. 40 Chetniks were killed, twice as many were wounded, and a wounded Chetnik was taken prisoner." This is what your command is saying. Is that what it reads?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to proceed with the order which reads: "Number 1, unit commander, through daily assessment of the situation, and the use of units in combat operations according to the" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that it is impossible to simultaneously interpret when the counsel is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter is having difficulty following you and has complained again about the speed with which you are reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, surely, but they have it on screens. They can easily follow it and interpret it from the screen. I will try to read as slowly as possible. It seemed to me that I was reading slowly but I can slow down each further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just two points to remark. There needs to be a foundation with this witness obviously that the document comes in. But I do have no objection if the whole purpose of this exercise is to have the document in. I have to objection to the document coming in. But so far I don't see any connection to this witness. I also note the time. So far, I don't have any redirect, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer will you be? You have utilized about - let me just ask the court deputy - the Prosecutor was two hours and 8 minutes, and I believe you have utilized just about maybe two hours. But I will hear from the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have utilized 2 hours and 4 minutes. One, we don't wish to reduce this to a mathematical equation, but you have had substantially the same time. If you have two or three more questions, we will allow you to put them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have between 10 and 15 more documents. I would need at least half an hour more than the Prosecution had, so I need more time. I'm going to omit the questions relating to the statement that I received only yesterday. However, I do believe that I should be allocated much more time than the Prosecution had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Hadzic, if you are feeling poorly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm very sorry to say that you will have to come back tomorrow morning, or if you are not well enough, then at some over time. But counsel is entitled to put his questions and to put his case to you. So you will, through the Prosecutor, let us know what your position is, whether you -- you're well enough to attend court tomorrow morning or at some other time. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, considerable time is eaten up these documents. And, as I said before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you spent a lot of time, too, Mr. Waespi, so you have to take some responsibility for this dilemma in which the witness finds himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I do. But the point I was making earlier is if the Defence wants to have these documents in we do not object, but it seems that the witness didn't speak to these documents as much as I thought he should, if he is shown the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
